reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Jordan ran to the art table at daycare. His teacher had put out big paper and glue. "Today we make snow pictures," she said. Jordan loved winter. Snow pictures were good.

Jordan squeezed lots and lots of glue. He stuck on cotton balls. They looked like soft white snow. But the glue was wet and shiny. "Can I take it home now?" he asked. "Not yet," said his teacher. "Wet glue drips. It has to dry first."

Jordan looked at the shelf. Yesterday's pictures were stacked there in a pile. He touched one. It was dry! "Where did the wet glue go?" he wondered. The picture from yesterday was dry because it had a whole night to sit. Maybe his picture needed a night too.

Jordan put his picture on the shelf. He added it to the top of the stack. "Now I wait," he said. "Later it will be dry." After nap time, he touched it. Still a little wet. So he waited more.

The next day, Jordan ran to the shelf. He touched his picture. Dry! The cotton balls did not move at all. "It dried up overnight," he said. "Yesterday it was wet. Today it is dry!" He carried it to his cubby. "Tomorrow I take it home," he said, "when Mama comes to get me."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Oliver walked home with a small puppy. The puppy was brown and soft. Oliver held the box very carefully. "Your name is Max," he said.

At home, Oliver wanted to play. He banged his drum. Max ran under the chair. Max would not come out. Oliver stopped the drum. Then Max came out slowly. "The loud drum scared you," Oliver said. "Loud sounds made you hide." Oliver sat on the floor. He was very quiet. Max walked to him and licked his hand.

"Good boy," Oliver said softly. He gave Max a nice soft blanket. He gave Max a bone to chew. Max chewed the bone and wagged his tail. Oliver petted him gently, so he would not hurt him. "I will keep the house quiet," Oliver said. Max fell asleep on Oliver's lap.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Florence ran to the block corner at school. Today she would build a nest for the toy bird. It had to be round and safe. "Watch out," said her friend Ben. "You must pay attention to the blocks you pick."

Florence picked the circle blocks first. She stacked them high. But the top circle wobbled. Then it rolled off! It rolled right across the rug. "Oh no," said Florence. "The circle rolled because it is round."

So she tried the square blocks next. She stacked them one, two, three. The squares did not roll. They had flat sides and stayed still. Florence put two triangle blocks on top, like a little roof. She made a round circle rug inside. Then she set the toy bird down in its nest. "Your nest is safe now," she said. The bird sat still and did not roll one bit.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Charlie woke up and peeked out the window. Snow was on the street. Snow was on the cars. No school today! It was a snow day.

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his warm coat. His mama pulled his hat down over one ear, then the other. Charlie went outside. He made three snowballs. He put them in his red bucket.

Then Charlie carried the bucket inside. He set it by the door. He wanted to save the snowballs for later.

Charlie played with his trucks. He played a long time. Then he came back to peek in the bucket. The bucket was empty! There was only water inside.

"Where did my snowballs go?" said Charlie.

The house was warm. Warm makes snow melt. The snowballs melted because the house was warm.

"I know," said Charlie. "Snow stays outside."

He went back out and made three new snowballs. "You stay here," he told them. "Outside is cold. Outside is just right."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Carter sat on the soft rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Mom was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too. Everyone wore different shirts. Carter's shirt was blue. Uncle Ben's shirt was green.

The team ran with the ball. Everyone jumped up. "Go, go, go!" they shouted. Carter clapped his hands too. But the room got very loud. Carter could not hear the man on TV. He could not hear the whistle. He tugged Uncle Ben's sleeve. "Too loud," he said. Uncle Ben nodded. "Let's cheer with our hands," he said. So they all clapped softly. Then Carter could hear the whistle. "When we yell, the TV is hard to hear," Carter said. "When we clap, I can hear it."

The clock on the wall showed it was almost snack time. Mom brought apple slices. Carter held one up to Uncle Ben. "Thank you," said Uncle Ben, and he took a big bite. The team scored. Everyone clapped, soft and happy. Carter heard the whistle one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Jasper wanted to play a new game with Mama. "Name your five senses," said Mama. Jasper did not know them yet. He wanted to do it well.

Mama held up a bright yellow lemon. "Tell me one sense." Jasper sniffed it. "My nose smells it!" "Yes," said Mama. "Smelling uses your nose."

Next, Mama rang a little bell. Ding, ding. Jasper pointed to his ears. "My ears hear it!" Then Mama let him taste the lemon. Jasper made a funny face. "My tongue tastes it. Sour!" Mama laughed with him.

Jasper looked at his hands. He touched the swing in the hallway. It was smooth and cold. "My hands feel it!" "Yes," said Mama. "Touching uses your hands."

"One more," said Jasper. He looked all around. "My eyes see you, Mama!" "All five," said Mama. She clapped.

Just then the swing bumped his leg by itself. Jasper blinked. "My eyes see that, and my hands feel it too!" he said. "Two senses at once, Mama!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ruby wants the big bear sticker. But first, the doctor has to do a checkup.

"Look here," says the doctor. He holds up a little picture. Ruby looks with her eyes. She sees a red bird! "Now be very quiet," he says. He puts a small tube near her ears. Ruby hears a tick tick tick inside. "That is your heart," says the doctor. "It goes thump!"

Then Ruby smells something sweet. It is the sticker sheet! She sniffs with her nose. "Yum, like strawberries," she says. The doctor laughs. "Stickers are not for eating. You taste with your tongue, and this is paper." Ruby sticks out her tongue to show him. "Say ahh," says the doctor. She says ahh.

Last, the doctor touches her neck with soft fingers. "Your neck holds your head up," he says. Ruby touches her neck too. Then the doctor says, "You did it! All done." Ruby picks the bear sticker. She holds it tight. "My heart went thump because I was so happy," she says.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Joseph was awake early for school. He ran to the window. It was sunny outside. "Short sleeves today," he said. But then the wind came. The tree bent over. The leaves flew up high. Joseph could not reach the big branch, but the wind could.

At school, Miss Kim said, "Time to go out." Joseph put on his sun hat. Outside, the wind pulled it off his head. It rolled far away. His friend Ana ran to get it. "Thank you, Ana," said Joseph. Then he looked around. Maya wore a hood. Ben wore a warm cap. Their hats stayed on.

Joseph had an idea. He pulled his hood up over his ears. The wind blew and blew. The hood did not move. "The wind took my hat," he said, "but it can't take my hood." At pick-up time, Joseph ran to his family. "Mom! The wind was strong today. My hood won."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe sat in the waiting room. She was going to get a shot today. Her tummy felt jumpy. She skipped all around her mom's chair, then sat down again. On the table was a special book about a bunny. Zoe touched the smooth pages. It smelled like paper and soap.

The nurse came in. "Sit very still," she said kindly. Zoe held her arm out. It wiggled like jelly. "If my arm wiggles, the shot is harder," Zoe said. So she pressed her arm flat on the table. She looked at the bunny book. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Zoe felt one tiny pinch, quick as a kiss.

The nurse put a soft bandage on. It had a star on it. "Now you can go to your dance class," Mom said. Zoe held her star arm up high. "Look what I got!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Xavier wanted to draw a big sun. Miss Amy had a tablet for him. But first the screen was black. "Press the little round button," said Miss Amy. Xavier pressed it. The screen lit up! "I did it," he said.

His fingers were sticky from jam at snack time. He tapped the green dot. Nothing happened. The green dot would not move. Miss Amy helped him wash his hands. Now his fingers were clean. He tapped the green dot again. The drawing app opened! "My hands were sticky," said Xavier. "Now they are clean, so it works."

He drew a big yellow sun. He drew red rays too. Miss Amy gave him a word for it. "Sun," said Xavier, and smiled.

Then it was time for lunch. Xavier pressed the round button. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, all by himself. "Bye bye, sun," he said. He waved at the tablet on the shelf.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Arya went to the library with Grandma. She wanted a book about spring. "Where is the spring book?" she asked. Grandma said, "Let's look on the shelf."

On the floor, a baby dropped a red ball. The ball was a circle. It began to spin. Then it rolled far, far away. The baby's lip went wobbly. Arya ran to get the ball. She gave it back. The baby smiled.

At the table, there were shape blocks. Arya picked a triangle block. It had three sharp corners. She pushed it on the table. It would not roll. She picked the circle block. It spun and rolled off the table. "The circle rolls," said Arya. "The corners stop it."

Then Arya looked at the books. Every book was a rectangle, with four flat sides. Rectangles do not roll. That is why books can sit on the shelf. Arya found a green book with flowers on it. "Spring!" she said. Grandma opened it. "My favorite season," said Grandma. Arya sat close and turned the first page.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Mohamed sat in his car seat. The sun was hot on his arm. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He moved his arm into the shade. The shade felt cool. "The sun makes it hot," he said. "The shade makes it cool."

"Papa, what is that?" Mohamed asked. He pointed at the cup holder. A cup of tea sat there. Steam went up, up, up. "Is it hot like the sun?" "Yes," said Papa. "Very hot. We do not touch it." Mohamed put his hands on his lap. He kept them far away from the cup.

They stopped at a big shop. Papa got out. Mohamed wanted to follow. But he waited and held the door. "Stay close to Papa," Mama said. Mohamed took Papa's hand. The parking lot was big and empty. "Where do we walk?" he asked. "Right beside you," said Papa. They walked in together, hand in hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Charles wanted to make a picture. He had orange paper and yellow paper. He wanted to glue them together. "Will the glue hold it?" he wondered.

He put glue on the orange paper. He stuck the yellow paper on top. He held it up. The yellow paper fell off! Charles looked at his hands. The glue was still wet and slippery. Hmm. Wet glue does not stick.

"I will wait," said Charles. He set his picture on the table. Then he went to eat his lunch. He had a sandwich and milk.

After lunch, Charles came back. He peeked at his picture. He touched the glue with one finger. The glue was dry now! He picked up the paper and shook it. The yellow paper stayed on. It did not fall.

"Dry glue sticks," said Charles. "Wet glue does not." He hung his picture on the wall.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Elias sat in a big chair at the mall. It was his first haircut. He put his toy car in his pocket. The hair lady put a soft cape on him.

Snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape, not on Elias. "The hair falls on the cape," said Elias. "The cape catches it." He watched the bits pile up. Then the hair lady brushed them all off. "All done," she said, smiling.

Elias got down and looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I like it," he said. Then they walked past the pretzel shop. "They cook the pretzels here," said Mom. "Can I smell them?" asked Elias. He sniffed the warm, sweet air. Mom bought him a pretzel and a juicy red apple. Elias held his toy car in one hand. He took a big bite of the pretzel. "Yum," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Mohamed wanted to play house with his bear. But the bear had a small wet spot on its tummy. "Why are you wet, bear?" he asked. Then he saw the answer. His water cup was tipped over. "You are wet because the cup spilled," he said.

Mohamed put the bear in the sun by the window. "The sun is hot," he said. "It will make you dry." The shadow of the curtain moved off the bear. Now the sun could touch it. Mohamed waited. He patted the bear. "Almost dry, almost dry," he said.

Soon the bear was warm and dry. Mohamed hugged it tight. "Now we can play house," he said. He gave the bear a pretend meal of blocks. "Eat your rice, baby," he said. The bear sat in the little chair, warm in the sun.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Arnaud loves the class robot. Yesterday the robot was loud. It rolled on the floor and sang songs. But today the robot is quiet. It sits still in the corner. Arnaud taps its head. Nothing happens.

"Why is it so quiet?" he asks his friend Maya. Maya looks at the robot. She opens a little door on its back. "Look," she says. "The battery is empty."

Arnaud wants to fill it up now. He takes the little plug. He pushes it into the wall. A small light turns red. "Now we wait," says Maya. "The battery fills slowly."

They eat snack. They play outside. Later they come back. The light is green now. Arnaud presses the button. The robot rolls out and sings its loud song again.

"It works now because the battery is full," Arnaud says. He claps his hands. "Tomorrow we will let it sing all day!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Isaiah stood in the school library. He wanted a book about a ball. But he did not know where to look. The shelves had so many books. He felt like crying a little.

Ms. Rosa knelt down beside him. "What do you want, Isaiah?" she asked.

"I want a ball book," he said. "I can't find one."

"Listen to the first sound in ball," said Ms. Rosa. "Buh, buh, ball."

Isaiah said it too. "Buh, buh, ball." Then he looked at the letters. He saw a big black B. "B!" he said. "B says buh!"

He ran to the B shelf. He pulled out a book with a ball on the cover. "This one starts with B," he said. "It says buh, like ball!"

Ms. Rosa smiled. "You found it all by yourself."

Isaiah sat on the soft rug. He hugged his book tight.

"Read it to me," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Bennett was at Grandma's house. Mom was there too. She had a big soft bag. In the bag was a small bundle. The bundle was Bennett's new baby sister. Her name was Ruth.

"Can we play ball?" Bennett asked. "Shh," said Mom. "Ruth is asleep." Bennett felt sad. He wanted to play with her now.

He waited. Ruth slept. He waited some more. Ruth slept some more. Grandma said, "Tiny babies sleep almost all day. They grow while they sleep." Bennett watched Ruth's little belly go up and down. Up and down, slow and slow.

So Bennett made a card. He used a pencil to draw Ruth. He drew one baby, two small hands, three little toes. Then he helped Grandma cut out a red paper heart. Snip, snip, snip. He waited some more.

At last Ruth woke up. She made a small sound. Mom put her on the blanket. Bennett held out his finger, very slow, very soft. Ruth's tiny hand grabbed it. She held on tight. "She likes me," said Bennett. "She held my finger because I waited."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Emmett sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself. "One, two, three, six," he said. That did not sound right. Daddy smiled and began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Emmett listened. The words always came in the same order. He tapped each pea and tried again. "One, two, three, four, five." So far, so good.

Mommy made a rainbow of fruit on his plate. Strawberries came first, then oranges, then bananas. "Can I teach the rainbow to count too?" Emmett asked. He pointed at each color. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All ten! He jumped in his chair. Then Daddy put one more pea on the plate. Emmett pointed at it. He knew no word for it. He got mad and stamped his foot. "There is no more counting!"

Daddy laughed softly. "After ten comes eleven," he said. Emmett tapped the new pea. "Eleven!" He said it two more times. Then he ate the rainbow, strawberry by strawberry.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
James sat in the playroom. He had a big pile of blocks. He wanted a tall, tall tower. First he made the bottom row. Then he stacked the blocks up, up, up. The tower got tall. Then it fell over with a crash.

James wanted to know how many blocks he had. He pointed at them. "One, two, five, nine," he said. That did not sound right. His big sister Mia came in. She patted his head. "Want to try a puzzle too?" she asked. She showed him a number puzzle with ten pieces.

Mia sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." James listened. The words came in the same order every time. That was the trick! He tapped each block as he sang. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten blocks!" said James. "The words go in a row, like the puzzle pieces." Mia smiled. He stacked the tower again, quick and careful. It stood tall. "One, two, three," he sang all the way to the top.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Aurora stood by the school gate. She held Grandma's hand tight. "I see Mommy soon," she said. Then a big bus went by. It ran through a puddle. Splat! Water hit Aurora's shoes. Her socks got wet. They felt cold and squishy.

"Oh no," said Aurora. "My socks are all wet." Grandma knelt down. "We can fix that," she said. She took Aurora to her cubby inside. There was a small bag inside. It had clean dry socks. Grandma helped Aurora pull off the wet socks. She hung them on her arm. "See," said Grandma. "Wet socks stay wet on your feet. Off your feet, they can dry."

Aurora put on the dry socks. They were soft and warm. Then Mommy came through the door. "My Aurora!" said Mommy. She gave her a big hug. Mommy touched the wet socks on Grandma's arm. "These need a bath and the sun," said Mommy. "Then they will be thick and fluffy again."

At home, Mommy dropped the socks into the tub. Aurora watched them swim like two little fish. "The water made them wet," said Aurora. "Now the sun will make them dry." Mommy smiled and kissed her head. "That's right," said Mommy. "Snack time now." They went to the kitchen together, hand in hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Carter went to the store with his mom. He wanted to pick apples for lunch. "Stay close to me," said Mom. Carter skipped beside the cart.

Then Carter saw a squishy orange. He reached for it. It sat on a high shelf with a big red sign. A man in a tall hat said, "Careful. That shelf keeps food hot. Touching hot food can hurt." Carter pulled his hand back fast. He looked at the steam rising up.

Carter saw the cold case next. His apple waited there, shiny and cool. He picked one up with two hands. "This one is cold," said Carter. "Hot things steam. Cold things feel like my fridge at home." Mom smiled. "Good thinking, Carter." They skipped to the checkout with one red apple.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Josephine sat at the little red table. She wanted to paint a frog. But there was no green paint.

She looked in the cup. She had yellow paint. Ben next to her had blue paint. "Can you share?" she asked. Ben poured some blue into her cup. It dripped, plop, plop.

Josephine stirred with her brush. Round and round she went. The yellow and blue mixed together. Now the paint was green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said.

She painted a big green frog. It had bumpy feet and a wide mouth. Ben clapped his hands. "Nice frog!"

Then Ben spilled his water. His paper got all wet. Josephine did not want to be mean. She gave him some of her paper. She gave him a hug too.

"Paint with me," she said. And they both painted green frogs.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Nova held a paper lantern. It was red with a gold fish on it. The morning had been long, and now it was dark. Papa lit the little candle inside. The lantern glowed warm and soft.

A big wind came. The candle went out. Nova felt sad, but she held still. Papa lit it again. The wind came back. The candle went out again.

Nova thought and thought. She put her hands around the candle. The wind could not get in. The flame grew small, then tall. It stayed lit!

"My hands stopped the wind," Nova said. "The wind made it go out. My hands made it stay."

Papa smiled and held his hands around his flame too.

They waited with all the other families. One by one, the lanterns rose up into the sky. Nova let go of hers. It floated high, a little star going up and up.

"Look, Papa! It flies because the fire makes warm air. Warm air goes up!"

The lantern grew smaller and smaller. Somewhere far above, it blinked once, like a wink.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Nova went to the big hall with Grandma. There was a long wooden table. Many people sat down to eat. Nova saw a box on the table. It was a present for Mr. Bean, because it was his birthday.

Before eating, everyone held hands. Grandma held Nova's hand. "We say thank you first," said Grandma. Nova did not know the words. She looked down and waited.

Grandma began. "Thank you for this food." Nova listened to each word. Then she said the next words in a small voice. "Thank you for our friends." Everyone smiled. Nova squeezed Grandma's hand. Grandma squeezed back.

The food was warm and good. Mr. Bean opened his present. It was a wooden spoon. Nova held hands again at the end. "Thank you for this day," she said, all by herself.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Everett was four years old today. Grandma's house was full of balloons. Everyone came in cars. They did not drive home yet. They stayed for the party.

The cake came out. Everett looked at it. "Where are my candles?" he asked. "I need four candles. I am four today." Grandma handed him the box. He took out one candle. He put it in the cake. Then he counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." There were four candles now.

Everett took a big breath. He blew. The flames did not go out. He was not mad. He waited a moment. Then he took a bigger breath. He blew again. All four candles went dark at once. Everyone clapped. "The candles went out because I blew hard," Everett said. Grandma cut the cake.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Elijah stood by the blocks at school. He wanted to line up first for snack time. But he did not know if he was first.

Miss Ada began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Elijah clapped along. He loved this song. He sang it in the car. He sang it in the bath. The words always came in the same order. After five came six, then seven, then eight, then nine, then ten.

Miss Ada pointed to the children at the door. "One," she said to Mia. "Two," she said to Sam. Elijah froze, very still, and waited. "Three," she said, and her finger touched Elijah. "Three! That is me!" he said. He bounced on his toes.

After snack, Elijah found a tiny horse on the rug. He held it up. "One horse," he said. Then he found a cow. "One horse, two cow," he sang. Sam laughed. "Cow comes after horse now," Sam said. Elijah giggled and hugged the tiny horse. "Ten more friends," he said, and pointed at the toy basket.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Bennett was at Grandma's house. It was pancake morning. Grandma said, "You can be the cook today." Bennett stood on his little stool. He was a big kid now.

First he cracked two eggs. A tiny piece of shell fell in. He fished it out with his finger. Then Grandma helped him measure the flour, the milk, and the sugar. Bennett stirred and stirred. He turned around fast to get the spoon. Now he felt dizzy. He held the counter and stood still. The room stopped spinning.

Then Grandma handed him a small spoon of baking powder. "Watch this," she said. She dropped a bit into a cup of warm water. It fizzed and bubbled up. Bennett's eyes went wide. "It woke up!" he said.

They mixed it into the batter. Grandma poured circles into the hot pan. Little holes popped up all over the pancakes. "The bubbles did that," Bennett said. "The bubbles come because of the baking powder." Grandma smiled and flipped one high.

The family ate the pancakes together. They were tall and soft and fluffy. Papa put honey on his. Bennett bit into his warm pancake. It smelled like sweet mornings. He licked syrup off his thumb and said, "I want to cook tomorrow too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Audrey ran into the pharmacy with Mama. Today was shot day! She loved the little bandages they gave after.

"Your turn," said the nurse. Audrey climbed up on the chair. She squeezed her arm into a tight ball. "Ow!" said Audrey. The shot hurt a lot on a tight arm.

"Try making your arm soft," said the nurse. "Like cooked noodles." Audrey let her arm go loose. It hung down like a wet noodle. The nurse poured a drop of medicine into the tiny needle. "Ready?"

"Ready!" said Audrey. She took a deep breath. Poke! It was done. "That one was small!" said Audrey. "My arm was soft, so it did not hurt much."

"You got it," said the nurse. She put on a bandage with a cat on it. Audrey held it up high. "Look, Mama! Noodle arms win!" Mama laughed and picked her up. On the way out, Audrey waved her cat bandage at the whole store.

story:
Peylon sat at the big table. Grandma put out paper and glue. Peyton wanted to make a sun. She squeezed the glue bottle hard. Glue came out in a big puddle. She stuck on a yellow circle. Grandma went to the next room to find scissors. Peyton waited.

The paper felt wet. The sun slid to the edge. Then it fell off onto the floor. Peyton picked it up. She looked at the glue puddle. "Too much glue," she said. "It made the paper all wet."

Grandma came back. She fished a small cotton ball out of the craft box. "Try this," she said. Peyton dipped it in the glue. She made one little dot. She stuck the sun back on. This time it stayed. Grandma gave her a fresh sheet of paper too. Peyton made one dot, then another. "Little dots work," she said. Grandma smiled and put her hand on Peyton's head.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jaxson sat at the dinner table. His doll sat in the chair next to him. Papa put a big bowl of soup on the table. Steam went up, up, up.

"Hot!" said Papa. "Wait a bit."

But Jaxson was excited. He grabbed the spoon fast. He sipped the soup. "Ow! Hot!" Jaxson made a grumpy face. His eyes got wet and sad. He put the spoon down. Why did the hot soup hurt him? Then he saw the steam dance over the bowl. Where the steam danced, the soup was still hot. He blew on the spoon. He blew and blew. The steam went away. He sipped again. Warm, not hot. Yum!

"Jaxson blew, so the soup got cool," he said.

Papa smiled. "Yes! Good blowing."

Jaxson fed a tiny sip to his doll. "Warm soup, doll."

He took another big sip and smiled.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rowan went to the cultural center with Mama and Dadu. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights. Long tables held many little clay lamps called diyas.

Rowan got to light one. Dadu held his hand steady. The little flame grew tall. Rowan smiled and smiled. Then the flame got small. Then it went out. "Oh no," said Rowan. "My lamp is broken."

Dadu shook his head. "Look inside," she said. Rowan peeked at his diya. The oil was all gone. The wick had nothing to drink. Dadu took a small bottle of oil. She poured some in. The wack soaked it up like a sponge. Rowan touched the stick again with the match. This time the flame stayed.

"The lamp went out because the oil ran out," said Rowan. Dadu laughed and hugged him. Then something surprising happened. All around the room, the big lights turned off. Hundreds of little flames filled the dark. Rowan's lamp was one of them. Mama lifted him up so he could see. "So many lights," said Rowan. "And mine is right there."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Connor ran to the playground. He wanted the red swing. But a girl was on it already. She swung up high.

Connor stopped and watched. He did not push. He did not yell. He waited. His shoes made a little line in the wood chips. The sun was warm on his head.

"Can I have a turn too?" Connor asked.

"Yes. You can come next," said the girl. "We can count to ten."

They counted together. "One, two, three." The swing went slow. "Ten!" The girl jumped off. Connor sat down on the red swing. It was hard at first. He pulled his legs in. Then he kicked out. He went up and up.

"Look at me!" he called.

Then a small boy came and stood by the swing. He waited just like Connor had waited.

"Your turn comes after me," said Connor. "We count to ten. That way it is fair for everyone."

"Can I count too?" asked the small boy.

"Yes," said Connor. "Count with me. One, two, three."

The swing went high. "Nine, ten!" Connor jumped down and held the swing still. "Here you go. Your turn now."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her team wore red shirts today. Grandpa waved from the bench. A gray squirrel sat by his shoe.

Sophie kicked the ball. A girl in a blue shirt ran to her. Sophie kicked the ball away. The coach blew a soft whistle.

"Why did you kick it away?" the coach asked.

Sophie pointed at the blue shirt. "You are not red," she said. "I pass to red."

The girl smiled. "I am on the other team today," she said. "Next time I will wear red too, if I join your team."

Sophie looked around. All her friends had red shirts. Ben had red. Mia had red. The ball came to Sophie. She kicked it to Mia. Mia kicked it in the goal!

Sophie jumped up and down. She wanted to cry, but happy tears. Grandpa hugged her tight. The gray squirrel clapped its little paws.

"Red is my team," Sophie said. "I always pass to red."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Olivier was at the doctor's office. He was not late. Mama said, "Good, we are early." Olivier wanted the plane sticker on the wall. The doctor kept it high up.

First the doctor said, "Close your eyes." Olivier closed his eyes. Then he could not see the plane sticker. He opened his eyes. Now he saw it again. "My eyes see it," he said.

Next the doctor held a little bell. She rang it by his ear. Ding! Olivier heard it. "My ear heard that," he said. The doctor laughed.

Then the doctor held a sticker near his nose. Olivier sniffed. It smelled like nothing. "Stickers have no smell," he said. The doctor said, "That is right."

Then it was time for the taste test. The doctor gave him a little cup. Olivier tasted it. It was sweet juice. "My tongue tastes it," he said.

Last, the doctor let him touch the plane sticker. It was smooth and shiny. "Can I keep it?" Olivier asked. The doctor said, "Yes. You were so good."

Olivier drew a picture on the paper table cover. He drew a big plane. Then he put his new sticker next to it.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zayn stood on the ferry with his dad. They were going to see Grandma. The wind stirred Zayn's hair. The boat went up and down on the waves. The car deck below smelled stinky, so they stayed up top.

Zayn had a bun in his hand. He wanted to save it for Grandma. But a little bit fell out of his fingers. It dropped down, down, into the water. A big white seagull swooped down and ate it. Then another seagull came. Then three more. Zayn looked at them. "The birds come because my bun fell," he said. Dad smiled and nodded.

So Zayn broke off one small piece. He dropped it on purpose. The seagulls came again, fast as a flash. Zayn laughed and clapped. He kept the big piece of his bun safe in his pocket. In his other pocket was an apple seed. He would plant it in Grandma's garden.

The ferry came to the other side. Zayn held Dad's hand and walked down the ramp. Grandma was waving by the gate. "I saved you a bite," Zayn said, "but the seagulls got the rest."

story:
Hannah stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. She had a small beanbag in her hand.

Hannah threw the beanbag. It hit the edge of the hoop. Then it rolled away. "Why did it fall out?" she asked. She looked at her hands. "My hands went down too fast." She tried again. This time she held her hands up and let go slowly. The beanbag flew up and dropped right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Hannah.

Then her teacher rolled her a big ball. Hannah reached out with one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. Her friend Sam said, "Use two hands!" Hannah held out both hands. The big ball came again. Both hands caught it and hugged it tight. Hannah laughed. "Two hands are better than one!" she said. She threw the ball back to Sam.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Asher sat at the craft table at the library. Miss Jo gave him white paper and a white crayon. "Draw a rainbow," she said. Asher drew a big rainbow. But he could not see it. The white crayon on white paper was invisible.

Asher felt sad. "My rainbow is lost," he said. The girl next to him was painting with bright colors. Asher's tummy was hungry, but he wanted his rainbow first. Miss Jo gave him a brush and blue paint. "Try this," she said.

Asher painted over the whole paper. The blue stuck to the paper. But the paint slid off his rainbow lines. His rainbow popped out, bright and shiny. "The paint won't sit on my crayon!" Asher said. The crayon kept the paint away.

The girl next to him smiled. "Do one for me," she said. Asher drew a big sun with the white crayon. He painted over it with red. The sun came out too. Then they shared crackers from Miss Jo's bowl. Asher took two, and gave one to his new friend.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
William sat in his car seat. He held his toy car and his red apple. His tummy felt empty. He wanted a snack now.

"Beep, beep," said the toy car. William drove it up his arm. Then the apple slipped. The apple did fall down, down to the floor. William reached and reached. It was too far. Now he had no snack, and his tummy growled.

"We will stop soon," said Mama. "Look at the farm." William looked out the window. One cow, two cows, three cows! One cow, two cows, three cows! The big cows ate green grass. William waved at them.

The car stopped at a little farm stand. There was a long wooden table. On the table sat milk, apples, and bread. "The milk is from the cows," said the farmer. William looked at the cows. Then he looked at the milk. "The cow makes my milk!" he said.

Mama bought a cold apple for William. His old blanket was in the bag, and it felt itchy on his legs, so he pushed it away. He bit the apple. Crunch! It was sweet. "The apple grows on a tree," said Mama. William looked up. He saw red apples in the green tree.

"One apple, two apples, three apples!" said William. Mama smiled. "Crunch," went William again.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Evelyn was at the big park. She could not find her blue bunny. "Where did Bunny go?" she said. Her tummy felt tight, like a rock. Mama knelt down beside her.

"We can look for Bunny," said Mama. "Let's go the same way we walked." So they walked back. Evelyn counted the spots. "One, the gate. Two, the swings. Three, the sand." At the sand box, no Bunny. Evelyn looked and looked.

Then she saw something. Bunny did not stay on the swing. It fell because the swing was moving. So Bunny fell off, down into the soft sand below. Evelyn dug with her hands. Her fingers touched something soft. It was Bunny! "The swing pushed Bunny off," Evelyn said. "That is why it fell!"

Evelyn picked up Bunny and hugged her. "I found you," she said. Now Evelyn would carry Bunny in her little bag. Then Bunny could not fall again. "Good idea," said Mama. Evelyn smiled big. "One, two, three," she said. "Three spots, and Bunny in spot three!" She gave Bunny one more squeeze and ran to the swings.
